data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel, CICT, MLT, Golden-Agri, Wilmar, CDLHT, FEHT, UltraGreen.ai
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 29):

Keppel : The asset manager and operator on Thursday reported a 20 per cent increase in its net profit for the third quarter ended Sep 30, 2026. Excluding its non-core portfolio for divestment and discontinued operations, net profit for “New Keppel” – the term the company uses to refer to its continuing core business – increased by close to 15 per cent year on year for the quarter. The increase in New Keppel’s profit was underpinned by stronger performance in its connectivity segment and steady earnings from its infrastructure segment, said the company. Shares of Keppel ended 0.3 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$10.13 before the results.

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT) : Its net property income rose 13.8 per cent to S$334.9 million and revenue grew 15 per cent to S$464.5 million for the third quarter ended September. The manager attributed the increase to contributions from Paragon, which it acquired for S$3.9 billion in July this year; Gallileo, its commercial property in Germany, following asset enhancement works; and its increased stake in CapitaSpring. The counter ended Wednesday 0.4 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$2.26, before the business update.

Mapletree Logistics Trust (MLT) : The trust had a flat second quarter, with distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.01816, up by 0.1 per cent, from S$0.01815 in the year-ago period. Distributable income grew 0.9 per cent to S$93.3 million for the quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, while revenue rose 1.4 per cent to S$180 million over the same period. Net property income rose one per cent to S$154.8 million. The increase was largely driven by contributions from the Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub redevelopment, an acquisition in India, organic growth in Singapore, and currency appreciation of the renminbi and Australian dollar, said the manager. Units of MLT ended Wednesday 0.9 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.07, before the announcement.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil producer reaffirmed its commitment to cooperating fully and transparently with the Singapore authorities over matters related to the Indonesian forest fires and transboundary haze. It issued the statement after a meeting with Singapore government officials over transboundary haze. The group added that it shares the Singapore government’s concern about the impact of fires and transboundary haze and welcomes the opportunity to engage constructively with the relevant authorities and independent assessors. Shares of Golden Agri-Resources ended 1.9 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.275 before the announcement.

Wilmar : The agribusiness posted a net profit of US$281 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, reversing from a net loss of US$347.7 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Core net profit for the quarter fell 25.2 per cent to US$267.3 million from US$357.2 million, even as revenue grew 13.6 per cent to US$21.7 billion from US$19.1 billion. The group said its food products segment was hit by higher raw material costs, and the feed and industrial products segment, by weaker soybean crushing margins. Separately, the group said the fires in Indonesia and transboundary haze have neither resulted in, nor is expected to result in any material operational, financial, legal or regulatory impact on the company. Wilmar closed S$0.02 or 0.6 per cent higher at S$3.27, before the results.

CDL Hospitality Trusts (CDLHT): The trust posted a 7.1 per cent year-on-year increase in net property income to S$36.7 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$34.3 million a year earlier. Gross revenue rose 4.1 per cent to S$72 million, from S$69.2 million previously, the stapled group said in an operational update on Thursday. The improvement was driven by stronger contributions from its UK, New Zealand, Australian and European properties. Stapled securities of CDLHT closed flat at S$0.70 on Wednesday.

Far East Hospitality Trust (FEHT) : The trust on Thursday posted a 6.3 per cent rise in its Q3 net property income to S$27.6 million, from S$25.9 million the previous year. The group attributed this rise to higher gross revenue, which stood at S$32.6 million, up 7.2 per cent from S$30.4 million in the year-ago period. The increase in revenue was mainly driven by stronger performance at Four Points by Sheraton Nagoya, which was supported by demand from the Asian Games 2026. Units of FEHT closed 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Wednesday.

UltraGreen.ai : Medtech platform UltraGreen.ai reported a 43.9 per cent growth in Q3 2026 revenue to US$44.6 million from US$31 million in Q3 2025 in a bourse filing on Thursday. This growth consisted of a 47 per cent increase from the US market from US$23.9 million in Q3 2025 to US$35.2 million in Q3 2026. The rest of world revenue contribution grew 32 per cent from US$7.1 million in Q3 2025 to US$9.4 million in Q3 2026. Shares of UltraGreen.ai closed up 7.6 per cent or US$0.04 at US$0.565 on Wednesday.

data.title: Chilli crab Ritz? How AI is shaking up Mondelezâs Singapore snack labÂ
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singaporeans are used to seeing Ritz crackers in the iconic red boxes on supermarket shelves, with their familiar cheesy, lightly salted flavour. But chilli crab, satay and laksa could offer a distinctly local twist on the classic snack in future.

These flavours are being prototyped at US confectionery maker Mondelez International’s technical centre in Singapore, where researchers are exploring new ways to keep the company’s products relevant to changing consumer tastes.

Two decades after its establishment, the centre is incorporating artificial intelligence into its R&D process to identify emerging food trends and develop new flavour combinations.

While some of these innovations may stay experiments forever, others have already made it to market in the region. A kaya butter-flavoured Ritz variant, for instance, hit Indonesian stores in May.

For the Nasdaq-listed manufacturer behind global staples such as Oreo and Cadbury, developing and commercialising new products is a core function of its Singapore Technical Centre in Jurong.

The centre is one of Mondelez’s 12 global technical hubs. Established in 2006 and expanded in 2018, it focuses on innovation in gum, candy, biscuits and other baked products, serving markets across the Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and Africa (Amea).

During The Business Times’ media tour of the centre, Marco Michielsen, regional R&D vice-president for Amea, said: “Singapore as a country ranks very high on the global innovation index, and that’s the main reason why we’re actually located here as an R&D centre.”

The firm has 61 people working at the local R&D site. 

Product innovation plays a role in the company’s efforts to grow sales.

Mondelez reported a net revenue of US$10 billion in the third quarter of 2026, supported by 2.1 per cent organic net revenue growth despite macroeconomic headwinds, driven by broad-based volume growth.

Its Amea segment recorded net revenue growth of 8.2 per cent in the quarter.

AI-to-oven pipeline

In the past, developing new flavours relied heavily on manual market research and repeated baking trials. Mondelez is now using digital tools to help identify promising ideas and streamline the development process.

For instance, the company has an in-house research platform that monitors shifts in consumer behaviour and identifies emerging local flavours. It also uses AI to analyse product sentiment and “make smarter flavour choices”.

In August, the Singapore centre also introduced an AI-powered Oreo-specific tool that enabled engineers to design and test virtual two-dimensional prototypes of the Oreo biscuit, before producing physical samples. 

The Oreo tool was first introduced to North America in the fourth quarter of 2025. Since the introduction to its Singapore centre, it has helped reduce the number of design iterations by about 20 per cent, Mondelez added.

However, Michielsen emphasised that AI serves as a support tool rather than the final decision-maker.

“What AI can do is provide predictions and patterns, but our scientists and sensory experts understand relationships between our products more than AI can at this moment,” he said.

Human expertise therefore remains central to the process, with digital tools helping researchers identify possibilities that they can then test and refine.

This collaboration is evident in Mondelez’s in-house innovation kitchen, where Harry Gui, R&D bakery chef for biscuits and baked snacks, uses trend data to develop complex flavour combinations.

“Then we translate (his flavours) into the lab, and eventually into manufacturing,” Michielsen explained.

Consumer shifts and commodity volatility

Beyond developing new flavours, Mondelez is adapting its Amea portfolio to address evolving health preferences and a fragmenting retail landscape.

The company aims to reformulate its snacks to reduce sodium, sugar and saturated fats, while incorporating whole grains and seeds such as quinoa and chia into its products.

At the same time, regional sales channels are shifting away from traditional supermarkets towards digital commerce and specialised chains, Michielsen told BT.

These changes come as the company grapples with supply chain disruptions and volatile commodity prices.

Mondelez’s gross profit for FY2025 fell 23.3 per cent year on year, largely due to an unprecedented increase in cocoa costs.

The company’s R&D team must therefore do more than respond to changing consumer tastes. It also has to find ways to adapt products and production processes as ingredient costs and availability fluctuate.

Michielsen noted: “One of the tasks that we need to do is to provide solutions for these supply chain disturbances, and we do that by assessing on a continuous basis our ingredients, processes, technologies and formulations.

“Our large-scale processes need to adapt – and they need to be adapted to (these) realities.”

data.title: Aseanâs fashion trade faces new survival rules
data.description:
FOR decades, Asean fashion grew by mastering a simple rule of survival: produce fast, scale volume, and win on price. This playbook built a regional fashion and textile industry on track to cross US$50 billion in market value.

Today, that has entirely changed. Mandatory disclosures on supply chain emissions are coming into effect across major import markets like the United States in 2027, while brands within the European Union will face stricter supply chain due diligence obligations starting 2028.

Suppliers and manufacturers who don’t meet – or simply don’t have the data to prove that they meet these standards will soon be locked out of global trade.

For Asean, which has emerged as the dominant manufacturing bloc for the US and EU, the new rule for survival is sustainability literacy.

The readiness gap

As it stands, while Asean is scaling in production, it is falling behind on accountability. Recent findings from the Singapore Fashion Council (SFC) highlight a significant opportunity to strengthen preparedness for these new reporting requirements.

For example, only 43 per cent of regional manufacturers currently track their greenhouse gas emissions.

Water consumption also appears to be a blind spot, where none of the manufacturers surveyed report that they measure their water consumption or have plans to begin tracking it.

In fact, fashion is merely the canary in the coal mine. From electronics to agri-food and automotive, heightened scrutiny on ESG makes one thing clear: no export-reliant industry in Asean will remain insulated from transparency requirements.

To survive and indeed, thrive, under these new rules, Asean companies must treat sustainability literacy as a commercial capability that needs to be actively built.

New rules for survival

The first rule is about starting with clarity, not perfection.

Businesses must familiarise themselves with emissions accounting guidance from regulatory requirements and recognised standards in the textile and apparel sector. This will help them to prioritise focus areas and select short-term goals that can already demonstrate success.

Many mistakenly believe that they need complex, costly carbon-accounting software right on day one. But they can start with simple baselines, like tracking office energy use or basic factory waste, and build internal capability before attempting to tackle more complex areas like the supply chain emissions of downstream partners.

Leveraging localised platforms like the Singapore Emission Factors Registry database or the new Sustainability Readiness Intelligence tool can also take much of the initial complexity and friction out of emissions reporting.

The next rule for survival demands collaboration.

Fashion and textile supply chains are tightly interconnected, where design decisions can contribute up to 80 per cent of a product’s environmental impact.

Co-creating with suppliers from the earliest stages of production allows brands to design out waste, extend product lifespans and keep materials in circulation longer.

A good example is zipper manufacturer YKK, which has developed its Revive series using zippers made from recycled plastic bottles. The design allows consumers to replace a broken slider easily from the top stop, rather than discarding an otherwise perfectly good jacket.

It is a practical illustration of how collaboration and thoughtful design can support circularity while helping consumers extend the lifespan of their clothing.

Customers are also key downstream partners in these efforts. Whether through take-back schemes or partnering local tailors for affordable mending services, brands and retailers can empower customers to keep their garments in use for longer.

Making circularity convenient is what turns consumers into active allies for waste reduction.

Finally, the third rule mandates that businesses communicate with credibility. Broad marketing claims such as “eco-friendly”, “green” or “conscious” are increasingly subject to scrutiny from both regulators and consumers.

The SFC’s data also highlights how credible, substantiated sustainability claims can be a key differentiator for Singapore enterprises seeking to build partnerships and enter new markets, both domestically and across Asean.

In today’s increasingly discerning marketplace, transparency and evidence-based claims, such as disclosing exact recycled material ratios and meeting recognised certification standards, are essential to building trust and unlocking business opportunities.

Honesty is fundamental. Partners and consumers respect realistic progress over impossible perfection. Demonstrating quick, achievable wins while acknowledging gaps builds market credibility that goes a long way.

Claiming Asean’s seat at the table

Ultimately, no brand, manufacturer or supplier can own this new playbook alone.

The scale of Scope 3 emissions and supply chain fragmentation across Asean demands a unified, ecosystem approach. The clock is ticking.

By moving from transactional vendor relationships to genuine co-creation, and from vague marketing claims to audited data transparency and traceability, the region’s fashion industry can turn a compliance threat into a lasting trade advantage.

The choice ahead is clear: rather than wait for global markets to dictate the future, we can claim our seat at the table and shape the evolution of sustainable fashion.

The writer is chief executive officer at the Singapore Fashion Council

data.title: Daiwa House Logistics Trust proposes to divest DPL Sendai Port, buy Hiroshima facility
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The manager of Daiwa House Logistics Trust announced on Friday (Oct 30) its proposal to divest DPL Sendai Port and use part of the proceeds to acquire DPL Hiroshima Itsukaichi Port.

In an evening bourse filing, the manager wrote that the divestment consideration for DPL Sendai Port amounts to 13.5 billion yen (US$85.8 million), representing a premium of 2.7 per cent above the average of two independent valuations of 13.15 billion yen, as at Sep 30.

The acquisition consideration for DPL Hiroshima Itsukaichi Port stands at some 8.2 billion yen, representing a discount of 16.7 per cent from an independent valuation of 9.9 billion yen, also as at Sep 30.

Why divest?

The trust is proposing to divest DPL Sendai Port to its sponsor, Daiwa House Industry, which was said to have made the only offer when the manager conducted an exercise to determine market interest in the property.

Located in Japan’s Miyagi prefecture, DPL Sendai had an occupancy of 31.9 per cent as at Sep 30, down from 100 per cent as at Dec 31, 2024, said the manager.

Occupancy declined further to 23.9 per cent in October.

The property had a weighted average lease expiry by gross rental income of 2.7 years as at Sep 30, and recorded a net property income of 246 million yen in FY2025, down from some 554 million yen in FY2024.

To improve its marketability through asset enhancement initiatives, large capital expenditures would be required, with an extended downtime and minimal contribution expected from the property, added the manager.

For these reasons, divestment was considered.

Why acquire?

Meanwhile, DPL Hiroshima Itsukaichi Port in Hiroshima is a high-quality modern asset occupied by blue-chip tenants that could enhance the trust’s portfolio quality, said the manager.

As at Sep 30, the property was fully occupied by two large third-party logistics companies. On a pro forma basis, this would improve the trust’s overall portfolio occupancy to 96.9 per cent from 88.5 per cent.

The property had a weighted average lease expiry by gross rental income of 2.3 years, as at Sep 30. It recorded a net property income of 471.2 million yen in FY2025.

The manager noted that it is a freehold logistics facility built with modern specifications, with a ramp for vehicles to get to the second floor, which would enhance cargo handling efficiency and offer flexibility in floor operations.

The property also has solar panels installed on its rooftop, with an aggregate capacity of 1.7 megawatts peak.

DPL Hiroshima Itsukaichi Port is described to be strategically located in a well-developed port industrial district, which makes it suitable for round-the-clock operations, said the manager.

It noted that the supply of large multi-tenanted logistics facilities is tight in the Hiroshima market, with the market-wide vacancy rate having been at 0 per cent since the fourth quarter ended Dec 31, 2023.

Being some 10 km away from the centre of Hiroshima makes the area suitable to serve consumption centres. It also offers proximity to a pool of labour, which is an important factor for tenants, added the manager.

Other benefits

The proposed transactions are expected to boost the trust’s net property income for FY2025 by 4 per cent, and that for the first half of FY2026 by 7.9 per cent.

Accordingly, the distribution per unit of the Reit is estimated to improve by 5.5 per cent for FY2025 and by 11 per cent for H1 FY2026.

After the transactions, aggregate leverage as at Jun 30, 2026 is expected to improve from 40.1 per cent to 38.3 per cent on a pro forma basis.

Said the manager’s chief executive Jun Yamamura: “The proposed transactions are expected to be distribution-per-unit accretive, and will also strengthen the balance sheet while providing (the trust) with financing flexibility to pursue further growth in future.”

The counter ended Friday at S$0.41, up 1.2 per cent or S$0.005, before the announcement.

data.title: Singapore is designing for a hotter future, but can it beat the heat?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The mercury is rising uncomfortably in Singapore’s concrete jungle.

The annual mean temperature could rise by up to 5 degrees Celsius by the end of the century, the latest climate projections from the Centre for Climate Research Singapore show. 

And as climate change raises background temperatures globally, urbanisation also adds a warming effect at the local level.

To meet its housing and infrastructure needs, the Republic has been clearing some secondary forests, which consist of regrowth over previously cleared woodland and make up most of the island’s forested area. These biodiverse ecosystems naturally mitigate urban heat.

To beat the heat, observers flag the need for urban planning that reduces land clearing, as well as adoption of heat mitigation and efficient cooling strategies to compensate for the loss of green cover. 

While Singapore’s heat mitigation solutions are largely mature, the challenge now lies in integrating them effectively at scale, watchers tell The Business Times.

Shrinking forests

Major forest loss in recent years includes clearance to accommodate new public housing in Tengah, which will be built on 700 hectares (ha) of secondary forest. However, the Housing & Development Board (HDB) has said that around 20 per cent of this land will be set aside for green spaces.

Plans are under way to clear two-thirds of the 23 ha Maju Forest in Clementi – also for public housing needs.

In fact, roughly 1,780 ha of Singapore’s secondary forest – equivalent to more than 2,490 football fields – was cleared in the past decade for development, one study has found. And the research shows that another 7,330 ha – one-tenth of the island’s land area – could also fall to the axe in the coming decade.

To build up Singapore’s green spaces, the National Parks Board (NParks) launched a movement to plant one million trees between 2020 and 2030. So far, more than 900,000 trees have been planted.

The campaign is on top of greenery replacement measures – such as replacement tree planting and adding plant life to urban areas – that are meant to offset development-related clearance.

Taking into account features such as nature reserves, parks, gardens and other managed vegetation, Singapore’s overall green cover now stands at more than 40 per cent. 

But scientists warn that urban reforestation cannot fully replace the climatic benefits of a forest and its mature canopies. 

Ongoing research by ecological design firm bioSEA and the National University of Singapore (NUS) shows that the value of biodiversity in the Republic’s green and blue spaces may have decreased by more than 10 per cent since 2011. 

“There is a need to prioritise mature green and blue systems, such as native-dominated forests, that have multi-tiered vegetation,” says Dr Anuj Jain, founding director of bioSEA. These provide “significantly higher biodiversity, carbon, cooling and air-filtration benefits” than urban streetscapes, parks and gardens.

Similarly, Associate Professor Yuan Chao from the NUS Department of Architecture tells BT that “no matter which solution we apply, we cannot go back to that benchmark” after a forest is cleared for urbanisation.

Pre-empting the problem

Singapore’s Meteorological Service reports that mean surface air temperature has risen by about 0.25 deg C a decade between 1948 and 2025. But the increase is not evenly distributed.

Buildings, roads and vehicles can trap and release heat into the environment, in what is known as the urban heat island effect. Research shows that this results in temperature differences of up to 7 deg C between the urban and less built-up areas of Singapore.

Still, Professor Matthias Roth from the NUS Department of Geography calls it “too simplistic” to say that Singapore is warming just because of deforestation or construction. This is because climate change, urban density and geometry, building materials, vegetation and wind flow “all matter”. 

To tackle the complex challenge, Prof Roth lays out three key steps for urban planners. First, reduce heat gain and the need for cooling. Second, design naturally cool and well-ventilated neighbourhoods. Third, supply any remaining cooling needs as efficiently as possible.

Ngiam Shing Shian, senior consultant at sustainability and impact advisory firm Aeterni.eco, notes that maximising the use of existing buildings could help reduce land clearing. 

This means urging developers to fully utilise existing facilities through retrofits where possible, rather than defaulting to demolition.

She says this would also involve the recycling of building materials that are already in circulation, and allowing more repurposing of spaces under current zoning policies. 

“These are not happening at the speed and scale that we need now, often because of the financials and business case. Hence, sufficient incentives and disincentives would need to be designed to shepherd companies in this direction,” adds Ngiam.

Meanwhile, it is possible to integrate nature into the built environment, too. Initiatives such as the Building Construction Authority’s Green Mark certification, NParks’ Skyrise Greenery Incentive Scheme, and the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s Landscaping for Urban Spaces and High-Rises programme aim to drive this shift. 

Having biodiverse microforests peppered around the city and allowing for healthy soil to be exposed to the air instead of being covered by concrete flooring have proven to be effective in heat mitigation. 

For instance, the size of the microforest outside City Development Ltd’s City Square Mall was doubled to 520 square metres (sq m) in January 2026 after a study showed that the green oasis helped lower temperatures by up to 5 deg C, compared with its surroundings.

Nature-inspired designs can also help to mitigate heat, Dr Jain of bioSEA says. His company specialises in “biomimicry design” solutions – its “elephant skin tile”, for example, mimics the folds on elephant skin to create microclimate-cooling surfaces with low-carbon materials. 

In his view, how available solutions “can work in tandem would be key... as opposed to (focusing on) one or the other”. “We envision some designs whereby our elephant tiles are able to integrate with (living green walls) where wildlife can create nests.”

Cooling needs 

Climbing temperatures drive up demand for cooling services, which account for 40 to 60 per cent of an individual commercial building’s energy usage and around one-third of Singapore’s overall power consumption. 

But waste heat from roads and infrastructure – including heat emitted by air-conditioning and other building cooling systems – is also contributing to the urban heat problem, Prof Roth notes.

“The challenge is not simply how to provide more cooling, but how to do so efficiently, sustainably and at scale,” says Jacques Boonen, Engie’s country manager and managing director of local energy infrastructures for South-east Asia. 

Alternative technologies that do not rely solely on air-conditioning are gaining traction.

So far, nearly 50 buildings in Singapore have adopted methods such as hybrid cooling, where air-conditioning is set at a higher temperature of 25.5 to 27 deg C and paired with fans. These methods can reduce cooling-related energy use by up to 50 per cent. 

Another option is district cooling, which involves the centralised production of chilled water that is piped to buildings for air-conditioning.

Heavy demand for cooling, particularly in commercial and industrial buildings, represents a significant opportunity for energy optimisation, says S Harsha, managing director for sustainable energy solutions at utilities supplier SP Group. 

SP Group operates the Marina Bay District Cooling Network, the world’s largest underground district cooling system. The network, which began operations in 2006, is expected to serve 50 connected developments by 2030, including Marina Bay Sands’ upcoming Integrated Resort 2.

The expansion will increase the network’s capacity by up to 10,600 refrigeration tonnes (RT) to more than 75,500 RT – or enough to cool 30 Grade A buildings in the Marina Bay district, based on SP Group’s data. 

Harsha notes that, compared with standalone chiller plants, district cooling delivers at least 15 per cent in life-cycle cost savings by eliminating the need for individual building maintenance and overhauls. 

Similarly, the centralised underground system that Engie operates at the Punggol Digital District is designed to yield roughly 30 per cent energy savings compared with conventional cooling. 

Boonen expects the district cooling market in Singapore to roughly double over the next decade from its current capacity of 323,000 RT – driven by demand from new townships, semiconductor manufacturing parks, hospitals and data centre campuses. 

As for scalability, he says it is “generally more straightforward” to deploy district cooling in new developments because the infrastructure can be integrated into blueprints from the outset. 

For instance, the incorporation of a district cooling system into the Punggol Digital District master plan let the cooling infrastructure be planned alongside retail, commercial and institutional developments, “creating a more integrated and efficient solution”.

Meanwhile, retrofitting existing developments for district cooling may be more complex, but it is “far from impossible”, he adds. 

The manager of OUE Real Estate Investment Trust has invested S$43 million to connect its commercial and office development OUE Bayfront to the SP Group’s Marina Bay District Cooling Network. Earlier this year, it announced that it would convert 2,100 sq metres of floor area previously used for chiller systems into prime office space. 

Boonen notes that ultimately, the “greatest potential” for district cooling lies in high-density, mixed-use developments where multiple buildings with significant cooling demand can be connected through a shared network – as in integrated districts that bring together commercial, residential, institutional, healthcare and transport infrastructure.

He adds that scalability depends on factors such as the cooling demand density, the mix of building types within a district, and the ability to coordinate infrastructure planning across multiple stakeholders.

Integrating solutions 

While district cooling is important for reducing the energy needed for cooling, “there is no single technological fix” for urban heat, Prof Roth notes. “Reducing urban heat requires a combination of measures operating from the building to the neighbourhood scale.”

For example, digital twins are virtual replicas of an asset that can use building management system data such as energy generation and consumption to maximise energy efficiency in real time. 

Matthew Chew, a digital twin system architect at mechanical and electrical engineering consultancy HY M&E, explains that digital twins allow cooling strategies to be simulated and fine-tuned before implementation. 

“The built environment is there for the next 40 to 50 years, so you can’t have an ‘oops’ moment because it’s expensive,” he says.

Other available technologies include specialised paints that reflect solar heat from building facades. Having found that these “cool coatings” can reduce ambient temperature by up to 2 deg C, HDB plans to introduce them to all public housing estates by 2030. 

But, more than ticking off a checklist of individual building features, heat mitigation requires stakeholders to coordinate short and long-term solutions seamlessly, says NUS’ Prof Yuan.

Indeed, conversations about heat mitigation technologies – such as heat energy-absorbing window glazing – must happen early in the design phase, notes Muhammad Khalil Shaiful Bahari, Boustead Singapore’s senior vice-president in the group technology office.

“Balancing sustainability goals with business values is essential,” he says, adding that “it’s not a zero-sum game”.

Drawing an example, he recalls “how office wear used to be – we wore shirts... and suits”. But as younger staff adjust to climate realities, “if they come in wearing T-shirts... that is much more environmentally friendly and comfortable at the same time”.

Based on research by the National Institute of Education’s Assistant Professor Wang Jingyu, between 2017 and 2024, Singapore’s “extensive urban green initiatives” helped lower the surface temperature of both deforested and non-deforested areas under daytime conditions. 

However, the cooling effect was weaker in deforested areas. 

“Urban reforestation is the most efficient solution to mitigate rising temperatures,” says Prof Wang, who also warned against “fragmented deforestation”.

Similarly, Prof Roth from NUS observes that urban development could amplify local warming and heat stress. “Preserving vegetation and designing developments to minimise heat storage and maintain ventilation can therefore help limit this additional urban heat,” he says.

data.title: US stocks: Nasdaq tumbles at open as Amazon, Intel add to AI spending woes
data.description:
THE Nasdaq opened at its lowest level in more than two months on Friday, after Amazon’s aggressive AI spending plan and Intel’s cash burn warning intensified investor concerns about escalating costs of AI infrastructure buildout and the return timeline.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 41.3 points, or 0.08 per cent, to 52,383.9 at the open. The S&P 500 fell 89.3 points, or 1.16 per cent, to 7,631.07​, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 592.2 points, or 2.26 per cent, to 25,592.486. REUTERS

data.title: Eurozone economy surges despite surprise slump in France
data.description:
THE euro-area economy surged in defiance of headwinds including elevated inflation and the selloff in bond markets, though France suffered an unexpected slump.

Gross domestic product across the 21-member currency bloc rose 0.4 per cent in the third quarter, twice the pace analysts predicted. Performances were mixed among its biggest members as Germany and Spain grew, Italy stagnated and France shrank by 0.1 per cent.

The overall outcome highlights Europe’s broader sturdiness, not just to the Iran war’s inflationary impact but to the heat waves and droughts that marred much of the summer. Still, the European Central Bank has flagged downside risks and could yet hike interest rates for a third time in December after standing pat this week. 

While inflation hasn’t spread beyond energy yet, policymakers in Frankfurt are wary. Separate data from France won’t reassure them, with consumer prices jumping 3.8 per cent in October, the highest level since late 2023. Inflation in Spain, despite easing a touch as anticipated, remained elevated at 4.9 per cent.

The jump in global bond yields is another drag, with France’s shaky fiscal and political position making it the region’s focal point. Its economy was already the euro area’s major laggard, only narrowly avoiding a recession in the first half amid soft domestic demand, falling investment and as hot weather hurt agriculture.

The outlook is bleak. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is in the midst of another parliamentary showdown over austerity, against a backdrop of social and political upheaval before presidential elections in 2027 where the far right leads polls.

“France’s economy is at a standstill due to a unprecedented convergence of external and domestic shocks,” Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Friday. “It needs to pick up. We need to restore confidence and for that having a budget is essential as that is what will allow us to bring down interest rates.”

German GDP rose 0.2 per cent despite factors including low water levels in the River Rhine. A public-spending spree on infrastructure and defence is generating optimism while carmakers may benefit from a European cap on Chinese hybrid-vehicle imports.

At the same time, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made fresh efforts to perk up growth through social-welfare reforms and attempts to lure private capital.

Italy’s government forecasts GDP will increase 1 per cent in 2026, helping finance some of the tax cuts Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has promised before elections next year.

She’s also asked Brussels for extra leeway of about 28 billion euros (US$31.3 billion) for energy and defence outlays. Any slowdown in growth would complicate other fiscal commitments, including getting the budget deficit below 3 per cent of output.

Spain, whose latest GDP reading was driven by domestic demand and trade, has shown significant resilience, with the central bank listing private consumption, job creation and population growth among drivers.

It sees growth of 2.6 per cent in 2026 and 2.2 per cent in 2027, comfortably above the euro area’s pace. It has largely shaken off political instability including Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez inability to pass a budget. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Bank of Japan declares victory in hitting price target, signals near-term hikes
data.description:
[TOKYO] The Bank of Japan kept interest rates steady on Friday, but declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could be as soon as December.

With underlying inflation having roughly hit the BOJ’s 2 per cent target, the central bank must focus on anchoring it around that level, it said, suggesting that its policy has entered a new, more hawkish phase open to hiking rates once every few months.

While refraining from pre-committing to a set pace of rate hikes, Governor Kazuo Ueda said the BOJ will debate rates at each meeting - including the next one in December - mindful that its policy has entered the new phase focused on inflation risks.

“It’s important to anchor underlying inflation around our target. That doesn’t mean we will just sit and wait. We will adjust monetary policy as appropriate so that underlying inflation becomes anchored around 2 per cent,” he told a news briefing.

The broad shift in outlook aligns the BOJ with its US and European counterparts eyeing near-term rate hikes to battle inflationary risks from the AI boom and the Iran war-induced energy shock.

At the two-day meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ maintained its policy rate at 1.25 per cent in a widely expected move, forgoing back-to-back hikes to spend more time scrutinising the effects of past rate hikes on lending conditions.

Hawkish board member Hajime Takata dissented to the decision to hold rates, instead proposing unsuccessfully a hike to 1.5 per cent.

In a surprise move that marks a further shift away from ultra-loose policy, the BOJ said it would accelerate its sales of exchange-traded funds from January to 860 billion yen (US$5.5 billion) per year from 330 billion yen currently.

“We saw the need to scrutinise a bit more economic and price risks, as well as financial conditions,” Ueda said, when asked why the BOJ decided to keep rates steady.

“But underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with our price target. Financial conditions remain accommodative. There are various upside risks. We must therefore be vigilant to the risk of inflation overshooting our target,” he said, keeping alive expectations of a December hike.

In a quarterly outlook report, the BOJ revised up its core consumer inflation forecast for the fiscal year ending March 2028 to 2.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent projected three months ago.

It upgraded its estimate for so-called “core core” inflation, which strips away the effect of fuel costs, for the next two fiscal years.

The central bank also said long-term inflation expectations were “moving around 2 per cent,” signalling its conviction sustained price and wage gains were becoming more embedded in the public’s mindset.

In the previous report released in July, the BOJ had said underlying inflation was nearing its 2 per cent target as long-term inflation expectations heightened gradually.

“Although its inflation forecasts remain broadly consistent with the 2 per cent target, the BOJ seems increasingly conscious of the possibility that inflation could overshoot,” said Kazutaka Maeda, senior economist at Meiji Yasuda Research Institute.

“Rather than sticking to the previously assumed six-month interval between hikes, it may now be contemplating increases every three months, making the December meeting a credible opportunity for the next rate hike,” he said.

Turning point

Declaring victory on the 2 per cent inflation target marks a turning point for the BOJ, which has spent most of its history battling low or negative price growth since gaining legal independence from the government in 1998.

Under former governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ deployed massive monetary stimulus in 2013 to pull Japan out of deflation and fire up inflation to the 2 per cent target.

Even after ending its mix of unorthodox easing steps in 2024, the BOJ has trodden cautiously in raising rates on the view underlying inflation – or price moves excluding one-off factors and driven by domestic demand – remained below target.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June – a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.

Most analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent in December, followed by further hikes next year. Their terminal rate projection centres around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent.

Rising prices, however, could weigh on consumption as they prod Japanese households, many of whom have never experienced widespread price gains in their lifetime, to seek discounts.

As its policy rate approaches levels deemed neutral to the economy, the BOJ has also stressed the importance of gauging how past rate hikes would affect domestic financial conditions.

The BOJ said financial conditions remain accommodative, suggesting scope for further rate hikes. But its report said real interest rates were “rising recently, although those for short-term zones remain low.” In the July report, it said real rates were “negative mainly in short- to medium-term zones.”

“The pace will depend much on upcoming data. We can’t decide in advance how many months we will spend each time before raising rates,” Ueda said on the timing of future hikes.

“We need to cautiously look at financial conditions as what we see now may not necessarily fully reflect the cumulative impact of past rate moves,” he said. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Clar, Seatrium, Sheng Siong, MPACT, NetLink NBN, Starhill Global Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 30):

CapitaLand Ascendas Real Estate Investment Trust (Clar) : The trust on Thursday recorded higher rental reversion in the third quarter of 2026 amid its drive to reshape its industrial portfolio. Its rental reversion for Q3 came in at 9.9 per cent, up from 5.2 per cent in Q2, and 7.6 per cent the year before. For the first nine months of 2026, rental reversion was 9 per cent. Portfolio occupancy improved slightly, rising  to 90.1 per cent as at Sep 30, up from 89.1 per cent in the preceding quarter. But occupancy was still lower than the 91.3 per cent recorded the year before. Units of CapitaLand Ascendas Reit closed unchanged at S$2.18, before the business update.

Mi Material: The chip materials company posted on Thursday an adjusted profit after tax of US$11.4 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. This came on the back of US$37.8 million in revenue, representing a 15.6 per cent increase from before. The Singapore-headquartered company attributed the improved profitability to “sustained demand for its semiconductor packaging materials”. Its shares closed at S$1.80 on Thursday, down S$0.02 or 1.1 per cent.

Sheng Siong: The supermarket operator posted a Q3 profit of S$44.6 million, up 1.9 per cent from S$43.7 million the previous year. In a bourse filing on Thursday, the company reported S$441.5 million in revenue, up 6.2 per cent from S$415.5 million before. The group attributed the higher revenue to a rise in total stores in Singapore, as well as improvements in comparable same store sales. Within the city-state, it now has 92 stores, up from 84 stores previously. Sheng Siong shares closed Thursday at S$2.80, down S$0.04 or 1.4 per cent.

Seatrium : The offshore and marine engineering group said on Friday that it secured a contract worth more than S$200 million from SBM Offshore to carry out integration works on a floating production, storage and offloading vessel for offshore developments in South America. Work is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 and be completed in 2029. Shares of Seatrium closed S$0.01 or 0.6 per cent higher at S$1.84 on Thursday.

Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust (MPACT) : Its distribution per unit fell 3.5 per cent to S$0.0194 for the second quarter ended September, from S$0.0201 a year earlier. This was mainly due to weaker contributions from its overseas properties, particularly in Japan, China and Hong Kong, as well as the absence of income from assets divested in the previous financial year, said the manager. The decline was partially offset by stronger performance at VivoCity mall, following its basement two revamp, and lower financial expenses. Units of MPACT ended Thursday 0.9 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.13.

Netlink NBN Trust : The mainboard-listed trust reported on Thursday distribution per unit of S$0.0274 for its first half ended Sep 30, some 1.1 per cent higher than the corresponding period the year before. The increased distribution attributable to its unitholders came despite a 2.2 per cent drop in revenue, which came in at S$202.6 million for the half-year, compared with S$207.1 million in the year-ago period. The distribution will be paid to unitholders on Nov 24. The counter ended Thursday flat at S$0.93 before the announcement.

Starhill Global Reit : The manager reported a 2.3 per cent rise in the Reit’s net property income to S$38.8 million for the first quarter of 2027. In a Thursday bourse filing, the Reit manager also recorded a 1.2 per cent increase in revenue to S$48.9 million, from S$48.3 million in the previous corresponding period. The Reit’s improved performance was mainly driven by stronger contributions from its Singapore retail and Australia properties. Units of Starhill Global Reit closed unchanged at S$0.495 on Thursday.

Wilmar : The agribusiness group said on Thursday that it will voluntarily engage, at its own cost, an investigations firm and a law firm from the Government’s panel of assessors to examine whether it has any involvement in or connection with the Indonesian fires contributing to transboundary haze. Wilmar said it will give the assessors access to relevant documents, personnel and sites, and is ready to begin the inquiry once the National Environment Agency (NEA) issues its directions. Shares of Wilmar closed S$0.16 or 4.9 per cent lower at S$3.11 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil producer said on Thursday that its Singapore subsidiary received a notice from the National Environment Agency seeking information relating to the transboundary haze. Its Indonesian-listed subsidiary also received queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange over forest and land fires. The group said it had not identified any material impact from the fires and haze. Shares of Golden Agri-Resources closed S$0.005 or 1.8 per cent higher at S$0.28 on Thursday.
